title: What Does Airplane Mode Actually Do?
sources: Apple Support 'Use Airplane Mode on your iPhone, iPad, Apple Watch, and Apple Vision Pro' (support.apple.com/108785): 'With Airplane Mode, you can turn off cellular and Wi-Fi on your device during a flight.' 'If the airline allows it, you can still use Wi-Fi and Bluetooth in Airplane Mode.'

CBS News Minnesota, 'What happens if you don't put your phone on airplane mode' (25 Feb 2025): airplane mode 'turns off a cell phone's radio frequencies, stopping its ability to make and receive calls, texts or use the internet'; pilot Randle Corfman: 'just a small buzzing sound apparently in the headsets of the pilots and the flight crew'; knows of no interference with navigation systems

FCC NPRM 'Expanding Access to Mobile Wireless Services Onboard Aircraft', Federal Register 15 Jan 2014 (WT Docket 13-301), para. 6 on the 1991 airborne-use rule: an airborne phone's 'signal would be received by multiple terrestrial cell sites in a given market, causing harmful interference'; 'a single handset could interfere with cellular systems in multiple cellular market areas simultaneously'

Popular Science, 'Why do we still have to use airplane mode?' (24 Dec 2024): FAA 2006 and 2012 studies 'found no evidence that cell phone signals interfere with aircraft systems'; a pilot described headset interference that 'felt like a mosquito'
Michael Tsai / Gaia GPS (2015): since iOS 8.3 GPS works in Airplane Mode ('pure' GPS, no A-GPS); GPS satellites broadcast and the phone's receiver only listens

lines.text: What does airplane mode actually do to your phone?
Well, your phone is basically a tiny radio,
always calling out to nearby cell towers.
Airplane mode switches that radio off,
and Wi-Fi too, though you can turn Wi-Fi back on.
lines.caps: AND *WI-FI TOO | THOUGH YOU *CAN | TURN WI-FI *BACK ON

lines.text: So why does the plane care?
Up high, one phone can reach lots of towers at once,
lines.caps: UP *HIGH | ONE *PHONE | CAN REACH *LOTS | OF TOWERS AT *ONCE

lines.text: which can jam the networks on the ground.
Pilots say it can make a little buzz in their headsets,
lines.caps: *PILOTS SAY | IT CAN *MAKE | A LITTLE *BUZZ | IN THEIR *HEADSETS

lines.text: but tests never showed it messing with navigation.
Here's the twist: GPS still works,
because your phone only listens to satellites.
Airplane mode doesn't make your phone deaf,
